title: Joe Rogan: Mars Landing Episode Planning
summary: Planning session for Mars-window podcast coverage. Agreed on a two-episode structure: a deep-dive episode recorded at Starbase in mid-October before the go/no-go poll, walking through the mission with hardware on camera, and a landing-week episode recorded within 48 hours of the first landing attempt with Gwynne Shotwell and Ashok Elluswamy as co-guests. Rogan declined to host live landing commentary — wrong format for failure scenarios — but will simulcast landing-day clips on X. Ground rules set: no embargoed dates revealed on air, failure scenarios discussed openly and in advance.
decisions: Two-episode structure: Starbase deep-dive in mid-October, landing-week reaction episode within 48 hours of the first attempt
Joe Rogan does not host live landing commentary; the live broadcast stays with the X/MrBeast production
Gwynne Shotwell and Ashok Elluswamy join the landing-week episode as co-guests
Failure scenarios are discussed openly on air before the landing, not spun afterward
Episode simulcasts on X with full-length upload day-and-date

action_items.task: Scout the Starbase recording setup — mobile studio in the high bay with Ship 2 in frame
Clear Gwynne Shotwell and Ashok Elluswamy for the landing-week episode and confirm what mission footage can air
Send the question list for the deep-dive so SpaceX can flag anything embargoed — content stays unvetted otherwise

transcript.speaker: Joe Rogan
transcript.text: Alright, so, we're not rolling right now, this is the meeting about the thing, which is already hilarious to me because you and I have never once planned an episode. You show up, we talk for three hours, sometimes there's a flamethrower. Now suddenly there's a producer meeting?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Because this one's different, Joe. In November we're landing five ships on Mars with robots on board, and the conversation around it is going to be enormous and mostly wrong. I want at least one long-form conversation on record that's actually right — the real engineering, the real risks, the real odds. Nobody does the three-hour version except you.

transcript.speaker: Joe Rogan
transcript.text: See, and that's why I said yes to a planning meeting, because dude — robots. On Mars. Walking around. Do you understand that for a guy like me this is the single greatest podcast subject conceivably possible? I've been doing DMT episodes for fifteen years waiting for this. Jamie, tell him the idea.

transcript.speaker: Jamie Vernon
transcript.text: The idea is we don't do one episode, we do two. Episode one: we come to you. Mobile rig at Starbase, mid-October, before the campaign starts — you walk Joe through the actual hardware, ship in frame, robots in frame if we can get them. Episode two: landing week, within a day or two of the first attempt, raw reaction while it's still fresh — whatever happened, triumph or crater.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Two episodes is the right structure, and Starbase in October works — come the week before the go/no-go poll, the high bay will have Ship 2 stacked and the first flight robots will be through vibration testing by then. You can meet one. It'll shake your hand. Gently. We tested gently extensively.

transcript.speaker: Joe Rogan
transcript.text: That sentence — 'we tested gently extensively' — that's the whole episode right there, that's the clip. Okay but here's the thing I actually want to push on, because everybody who comes on this show sells me the highlight reel. I don't want the highlight reel. What are the odds, real odds, that this whole thing faceplants? And will you say that number on air?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I'll say it on air, and here it is now: entry, descent and landing at Mars with a vehicle this size has never been done, our aero data is simulation plus extrapolation, and I'd put maybe sixty to seventy percent on at least one ship landing intact, way lower on all five. First ships are instrumented like flying wind tunnels because we expect to learn from losses. If someone tells you a first Mars campaign has no failure modes, they're lying or selling something.

transcript.speaker: Joe Rogan
transcript.text: That — okay, that's why this works. Because here's my rule for this one, and Jamie back me up, we talked about this before you got here. The failure conversation happens before the landing, on air, in full. Because if we only do the episode where it works, we're a commercial. And if it fails and THEN we talk, it's spin. The odds go on record in October. That's the deal.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: That's the deal and honestly it helps me — I've been telling my own comms team the same thing. Public framing is 'first attempt, success is one robot walking off one ship.' You putting the sixty-seventy percent number into a three-hour conversation does more expectation-setting than fifty press releases.

transcript.speaker: Jamie Vernon
transcript.text: Okay, logistics from my side. Starbase mobile rig — I need a site visit by mid-September to figure out power, acoustics, and whether we can actually shoot in the high bay, because that room is going to echo like a cathedral. And I need to know now what the camera restrictions are. Last time we shot at a SpaceX facility there were three lawyers walking backwards in front of every shot.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: It's gotten better — ITAR still applies so there's a list, mostly engine internals and some avionics, but the high bay with a stacked ship is fine, we show that on our own streams. I'll have someone walk you through the restricted list during the site visit. September 15 or earlier works for the scout.

transcript.speaker: Joe Rogan
transcript.text: Now the landing-week episode. Here's what I want and you're going to have to pull strings. I don't want just you. You're great, but I've had you — what, six times? For landing week I want the people who actually flew it. Give me Gwynne Shotwell. Everybody says she's the adult in the room, I want three hours with the adult in the room. And the robot guy, the one who runs the AI — because the robot walking off that ship on its own with a twenty-minute light delay, no joystick, that's the part nobody understands is insane.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Gwynne and Ashok. Gwynne will be sleep-deprived and completely unfiltered, which is the best version of her, and Ashok can explain autonomy at light delay better than anyone alive. I'll clear both of them by October 1, plus what mission footage we can hand you for the episode — entry cameras, landing burns, whatever the relay constellation actually gets down. One caveat: if the relay deployment slips, the good imagery might take a day or two to arrive, so the episode timing may need to flex around when the pictures exist.

transcript.speaker: Jamie Vernon
transcript.text: We can flex — 'within 48 hours of the attempt' is the target, and we'll hold the week open. Next thing: the live question. Everyone's going to assume Joe does live commentary during the actual landing. I've already had two networks call about it.

transcript.speaker: Joe Rogan
transcript.text: And the answer's no, and Elon, I want to explain why because it's not modesty. Live event commentary is a skill I don't have and don't want — if a ship crashes on live TV, you need either a NASA-voice professional or silence, and what you absolutely don't need is me going 'oh no, oh NO' to a hundred million people. That moment belongs to mission control audio. I'll watch like everybody else, then we do the episode where we actually process it. That's what long-form is FOR.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Completely right call, and the live side is covered anyway — there's a whole production planned on X for landing day, Jimmy Donaldson's involved, it'll be its own animal. What we'd want from you on landing day is simple: simulcast clips, and the October episode drops its full version on X day-and-date so the deep-dive is sitting there when a hundred million people suddenly want context.

transcript.speaker: Joe Rogan
transcript.text: Day-and-date on X is fine, we do that already. MrBeast doing the live thing is perfect by the way — that kid understands spectacle at a level that's honestly a little frightening. Okay, my last item, and this is the important one. Nobody vets my questions. I'll send Jamie's question list ahead so your people can flag actual embargo stuff — dates you haven't announced, whatever ITAR is grumpy about — but no message discipline, no talking points, no comms person in my ear. The moment it's vetted, it's worthless, and everyone can smell it.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Agreed without hesitation — the unvetted thing is why your show matters and frankly why I keep coming back. Flag list for embargoes only, everything else is fair game, including the stuff you think I'll dodge. I've noticed I'm more honest in hour three anyway, it's a stamina exploit and you know it.

transcript.speaker: Joe Rogan
transcript.text: It's a feature, not a bug, and everybody's version of hour-three honesty is why the format works. Alright — Jamie scouts Starbase by September 15, we record mid-October before your go/no-go thing, you clear Gwynne and the robot guy by October 1, questions go over by the 5th for embargo flags only, landing-week episode within 48 hours of the attempt, everything simulcasts on X. Dude. Robots. On Mars. I'm going to think about nothing else for four months.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Four months for you, every waking minute for me. See you at Starbase in October, Joe — bring the good questions, and don't touch anything that says flight hardware.
